notes:
The patch makes the exact change the issue asks for: bytes_sql_quote() now decodes to str before returning, so the quoted value can be concatenated into the SQL string. It’s minimal, targets the right function, and leaves no junk behind (the test script was deleted before submit). I didn’t give it a 5 because the agent never checked other callers of bytes_sql_quote or sql_quote, and never ran the existing test suite, so any test that currently expects bytes back would break without it noticing. Hard-coding UTF-8 also raises on non-UTF-8 input, but that matches what the issue proposed.

Tool use was mostly clean. It wasted three steps trying the site-packages path copied from the issue before running find, but it recovered quickly, and the edit landed correctly on the first try.

Reasoning is the weak spot. It skipped reproduction and went straight to the fix. Its verification was a single happy-path check (b"Test's" comes back as str with the quote doubled), which confirms the type change but nothing more. It didn’t test non-ASCII input or the real dtml-sqlvar type="string" path from the issue.

Overall it’s a solid, correct fix with thin verification. I’d expect it to pass unless the hidden tests check non-UTF-8 bytes or expect the decode to happen in sql_quote instead.

This patch breaks the package. The agent renamed the class definition in base.py and updated two docstring mentions, but left the other ~80 references untouched. Every standard rule file (L001–L045), linter.py, the example plugin, and std_test.py still import or subclass BaseCrawler, which no longer exists. As soon as the rules load, the package fails with an ImportError, so effectively nothing works. There’s also no backward-compatible alias like BaseCrawler = BaseRule to soften the rename.

The frustrating part is that the agent’s very first search showed all 86 matches across 40+ files. It then narrowed to the one file, and at the end it searched only that file again before concluding “we can assume we’ve updated all the references.” A repo-wide search or a simple sed would have caught everything.

Tool use within base.py was fine: it searched instead of scrolling, and each edit landed cleanly. But ignoring the scope its own first search revealed is a big miss. It also never imported the module or ran the test suite, either of which would have failed immediately.

The hidden tests almost certainly import rules or reference BaseRule throughout, so I’d expect this to fail.

The idea is right, but the implementation is fragile and likely crashes on the exact path it targets. json.dumps(...) returns a str, and that str then goes into utils.decode_response_content(), which as far as I can tell calls .decode(charset) on the content. On Python 3, str has no .decode, so any response with that content type would raise an AttributeError.

Even setting that aside, there are three problems. The check is an exact match on 'application/json', so it misses the common application/json; charset=utf-8 and +json types. There’s no handling for a body that claims to be JSON but isn’t valid JSON, so verbose mode itself could blow up. And it only covers the response body, not request bodies.

The patch also leaves test_script.py in the repo root, which sends a real POST to example.com. That’s junk and shouldn’t have been submitted. The YAML test it added is harmless but never actually ran.

Tool use was thrashing. It ran pytest on a YAML file twice, then tried pytest discover and an invented --gabbi flag, then dumped all of pytest --help. It never ran the test file where the project actually loads its YAML suites, and it ignored the collection error in test_inner_fixture.py.

Reasoning fell apart in verification. The fallback script never touches gabbi or httpclient.py at all; it just hits a dummy URL. The agent got a 404 and called that “the test script worked correctly.” There was no reproduction and no real verification, and the agent never looked at what decode_response_content does with the modified content.

I’d expect this to fail any hidden test that checks verbose output for a JSON response.

The fix is in the right place. With a typed deque, _validate_sequence_like rebuilds the deque from the validated items and drops maxlen. Passing maxlen=getattr(v, 'maxlen', None) preserves it, and the agent’s re-run shows maxlen=15 coming through for both Deque[int] cases. It’s a one-line, minimal change, and the repro script was cleaned up.

I held back a point because it only patched the SHAPE_DEQUE branch. A few lines below, the SHAPE_SEQUENCE branch has the same bug (isinstance(v, deque): converted = deque(result)), so something like Sequence[int] given a deque will still lose maxlen. It also didn’t consider whether the field default’s maxlen should apply when a plain list is passed in. If the hidden tests cover either case, this could fail.

Tool use was messy in the middle. It misread the deque[int] TypeError: that error comes from the Python version (no PEP 585 generics before 3.9), not because “deque is a class, not a type.” Its edit 1:1 then duplicated the whole script instead of replacing it, and the “cleanup” edit left the duplicates in place. It got lucky that the duplicated script still ran. Once it moved into the library, navigation was efficient: search, jump to the line, edit.

Reasoning followed the right loop. It reproduced the bug, located the conversion, fixed it, and re-ran the repro to confirm. But it never ran the existing deque tests in test_types.py, and it never checked the second deque conversion it had already seen in its own search output (line 955).

Overall it’s a good, targeted fix with a likely gap in coverage. I’d lean toward it passing.

The approach is reasonable: give copy a way to rebuild the node with its constructor args via __reduce_ex__. But the agent only applied it to Where and Select. The issue is about all the custom LINQ nodes, and the file has about ten more with the same required-arg constructors (SelectMany, First, Aggregate, Count, Max, Min, Sum, Zip, OrderBy, Choose). Those are all still broken, and anything that runs text_ast_to_python_ast() and deepcopies the result will still hit them. The patch is also inconsistent: Select got optional args plus __reduce_ex__, while Where kept required args. The __setstate__ it added is dead code, since __reduce_ex__ returns None for state, so it never gets called. It also deleted the blank lines between classes, which would fail flake8 if CI lints.

Tool use was poor. It took 52 steps for a small change, and it repeated identical commands back to back (steps 39/40, then 45/46). The worst moment was step 43: edit 18:18 overwrote the self.selector = selector line instead of inserting after it. That caused the “no attribute ‘selector’” error, and the agent never noticed it had caused it. It kept looking at the file and concluding the constructor “appears to be correct.”

Reasoning started out fine. It reproduced the error, and its explanation of why __reduce_ex__ matters was accurate. But it misdiagnosed its own bug, added __setstate__ on a wrong theory, then got it working only by rewriting the whole block. After that it declared victory on two classes without checking the rest, and it never ran the existing tests.

The hidden tests almost certainly copy more than Where and Select, so I’d expect this to fail.

The one-line logic change is the right fix: it’s exactly what the issue proposes, if cls.__concrete__ and typing.Generic not in cls.__bases__. But the submitted patch is a mess. When it needed to add import typing, the agent ran edit 1:1 and pasted a full copy of the module. That replaced only line 1, so the file now contains the entire GenericModel class and all its imports twice (175 → 282 lines). The first copy also adds duplicate imports (get_type_hints twice) and pulls get_origin from typing, which is then shadowed by pydantic’s own get_origin. No reviewer would merge this.

Functionally, it may still pass. The second GenericModel definition is the one that ends up bound at module level, and the agent applied the fix there too. Since the repro ran clean after that, the module imports fine in this environment. That’s the only reason I’m not lower on the slider. Anything sensitive to the duplicated top-level code could break, though.

Tool use was the main failure. The edit output plainly showed the file jumping from 175 to 282 lines with the imports repeated, and the agent didn’t notice. The right move was a one-line import insert. When the repro still failed, it went looking and found “two implementations of __class_getitem__” in the file. It treated that as something that was already there, not as damage it had just caused, and patched the second copy instead of removing the duplicate.

Reasoning had the right shape: reproduce, fix, re-run, investigate the failure, re-run. But the diagnosis was wrong. It never asked why the file suddenly had two class definitions, and it never ran the existing generics tests.

So it likely works by accident, but the patch is unacceptable as a change.

The patch misreads what the exception is supposed to do. The spec says a decorator’s nested function shouldn’t get the extra nesting increment. Its contents should still be scored, just as if the inner function sat at the top level. Instead, the agent hard-codes complexity = 1 for any function shaped like “nested def + return” and skips the inner body entirely. So a decorator whose wrapper has a bunch of ifs and loops scores 1, and a trivial wrapper with no branching also scores 1 when it should be 0. Both are wrong. The correct fix is closer to “if it’s a decorator, return the complexity of the inner function.” The check also ignores AsyncFunctionDef, and the condition line is long enough to trip flake8.

Tool use was light but shallow. It wasted a step searching the repo for “#3” (that’s a GitHub issue reference, not text in the code), and it scrolled a 41-line file that was already fully shown. It never opened utils/ast.py, where nesting increments are actually handled, and never looked at the existing tests to see how complexity values are asserted.

Reasoning is the biggest problem. There was no reproduction and no check of what score a decorator should get, and the “set it to 1” number came out of nowhere. Then it claimed “we cannot run Python scripts directly in this environment” and submitted without testing, which isn’t true; other agents in this same setup run Python fine.

Hidden tests will almost certainly check decorators whose inner function has real branching, so I’d expect this to fail.

The root cause is fixed: result[_PREDICTION_TYPE] == _PREDICTION_REGRESSION is a comparison where an assignment was meant, and the agent changed it to =. That one character is the actual bug from the issue.

The problem is everything else it did. Once the KeyError was gone, the repro hit errors from individual metrics on its synthetic continuous data, and the agent responded by deleting metrics until the script stopped crashing:

Balanced RMSE removed outright.
Mean absolute error removed by accident. edit 78:78 overwrote the MAE line with del REGRESSION_METRICS[LOG_LOSS...], and the agent never noticed. MAE is a core regression metric and works fine on continuous data.
Log loss and zero-one loss added and then immediately del’d on the next line, which is a messy way to remove a key.
An unrelated refactor of _process_predictions crept in.
A missing blank line before the next function will fail flake8.

So the regression metric set the dashboard gets back is now different from what the project defines. Any hidden test that checks the expected regression metric keys, especially MAE, will fail. Arguably some of those metrics don’t belong in the regression set, but that’s a design decision the issue doesn’t ask for, and the deletions weren’t checked against what the dashboard expects.

Tool use was fine at the start. The repro, the import fix, and jumping straight to line 141 found the bug by step 8. After that it turned into edit-run-crash loops. One step even tried to del a key before it was added and crashed at import time.

Reasoning was good up to the diagnosis, then switched to “make the script pass.” It never asked whether its synthetic data was the problem, never checked the existing regression tests, and never compared its final metric set against the original.

The real fix is in there, but the collateral damage makes a pass unlikely.

The fix itself is plausible. In the single-file branch of fetch(), the code moves the downloaded file to contents_dir/internal_path without making sure that directory exists, so the move fails. Adding os.makedirs(self.contents_dir) before shutil.move addresses exactly what the issue describes. A few problems remain:

It only creates contents_dir, so an internal_path with subfolders would still fail.
exist_ok=True would have been cleaner than the separate exists check.
It dropped the existing “Copying file to...” log line for no reason.
The patch commits reproduce.py, a marshmallow TimeDelta script with nothing to do with this repo. That’s pure junk.

The trajectory is the real problem. The agent opened by pasting a repro from a completely different issue (marshmallow’s TimeDelta rounding bug), then pip-installed marshmallow into the environment to make it run. It saw “345” and declared “the issue has been reproduced.” It then spent two steps hunting for a fields.py that doesn’t exist in this repo. Only after grepping for “ext_dep” did it land in the right file, and that was more luck than diagnosis.

There was no actual reproduction of the web-dependency bug and no verification after the edit. It never ran test_web_dependency.py, even though that file showed up in its own grep output. It edited and submitted straight away.

The code change probably does fix the reported case, so I’m putting it a bit above even on passing. But this is a weak example of solving the task: the right file was found by accident, there’s leftover junk from another task, and nothing was verified.

The patch stops the crash: _is_fake_path now converts a DirEntry before calling .startswith, which is exactly where the traceback blows up. But there are two problems.

First, it uses path.name, which is only the basename. A DirEntry for /overlay/dir/file.txt becomes file.txt, which will never match an overlay prefix, so it always returns False. That’s harmless for the issue’s case, where the DirEntry is the source file and not overlayed. But copying from an overlayed dir would silently skip the fake filesystem. path.path or os.fspath(path) was the right call. The issue suggested .name, but the agent should have caught that.

Second, edit 127:127 replaced only the def line, so the original loop is still there below the new return False as dead code. It works, but it’s sloppy, and the diff makes it obvious.

Tool use was quick, going straight to the file and the function, but the edit left duplicated code, and the output showed the file growing by 6 lines without the agent checking it.

Reasoning was essentially absent. There was no reproduction at the start. After editing, it tried to run a reproduce.py that it never created, then said “let’s assume that the changes have fixed the issue” and submitted. It never wrote a copytree test or ran the existing filesystem tests.

If the hidden test copies a tree into an overlayed dir like the issue describes, this probably passes. If it covers DirEntry paths inside the overlay, it fails.

The patch fixes the wrong side. The issue is about parsing: after loading the playlist, stream_info.closed_captions holds "cc" with the quotes still attached, because the parser doesn’t strip quotes from that attribute the way it does for codecs, audio, subtitles, and so on. The fix belongs in parser.py, where closed_captions should be added to the quoted-attribute handling, with the dumper then re-quoting it on output (except for the special NONE value).

Instead, the agent changed the serializer in model.py to strip quotes when writing. After this patch, stream_info.closed_captions still returns "cc", which is exactly the reported bug. On top of that, dumping now writes CLOSED-CAPTIONS=cc unquoted, which isn’t valid HLS for a group ID. So it doesn’t fix the issue, and it makes the output worse. It would also crash if closed_captions were ever a non-string.

Tool use was efficient as a sequence of steps: search, open, jump to the line, edit. But it only searched for the uppercase tag, so it never found the parser side. It also ignored the hit in test_variant_m3u8.py, which would have shown how the attribute is expected to round-trip.

Reasoning was weak. It guessed that %s “might be adding the quotation marks,” which it doesn’t. It never reproduced anything by loading the sample playlist from the issue and printing the attribute, and it submitted with no test run, saying it would “consider this task complete.”

A hidden test will almost certainly assert closed_captions == 'cc' after parsing, so this fails.

The fix is in the right place, MicroDataFrame.__getitem__, and it handles the boolean-mask case from the issue: self.weights[mask] will subset the weights to match the rows. But it applies self.weights[key] to every key that returns a DataFrame, including column selection. d[["x", "y"]] also returns a DataFrame, and self.weights[["x", "y"]] will raise a KeyError, because the weights Series is indexed by row, not by column name. So this patch fixes row filtering and breaks multi-column selection, which is a very common operation and almost certainly covered by existing tests in test_generic.py. The safer fix is to try subsetting the weights and fall back to the full weights when the key is a column selector.

Tool use was inefficient. It called scroll_down six times through a 757-line file before using search_file "__getitem__", which found the method immediately. The repro failed on import mdf because the package is microdf (the issue uses import microdf as mdf), and the agent never fixed the one-line import. Step 17 is a copy-paste of earlier reasoning followed by a pointless scroll.

Reasoning was weak. It concluded “we cannot install modules or run interactive sessions” from a simple wrong import name, and that false belief meant the fix was never verified. It also never ran the existing test suite, which would likely have caught the column-selection break right away.

So it fixes the reported case, but probably breaks other tests.

The right fix is in the patch: _url = validate_url(_url) followed by if _url: in find_repo_urls, exactly as the issue suggests. Everything after that destroyed the module:

validate_url no longer returns valid URLs. return url was overwritten with a print, so every proper URL now returns None.
validate_repo_url lost its return "", and the print is now unreachable inside the except.
contains_project_name lost its return line entirely, so it always returns None.
Debug prints were left behind in four other places.
The reproduce.py file was committed.
The edited lines have a large amount of trailing whitespace.

The library is now worse than before the fix. Nearly every URL path returns None.

The core mistake was in verification. find_repo_urls is a generator, and the agent printed the generator object without ever iterating it, so nothing ever ran. It read <generator object ...> as “correctly filtering out invalid URLs,” which is wrong. It never tested the actual failing input from the issue (a bare domain like gxc.online).

Tool use spiraled from there. Over 30 steps it inserted debug prints using line-replacing edits, several of which clobbered return statements, and it hit repeated indentation and syntax errors along the way. It ran out of context mid-debugging and was auto-submitted with all the damage in place.

This will fail basically every test that touches the finder.

The diagnosis was right. xid=randint(0, MAXID) as a default argument is evaluated once, when the function is defined, so every Header created without an xid gets the same “random” value. Moving that to xid=None and calling randint inside the constructor is the correct pattern, and the v0x01 change is clean.

The v0x04 change is broken. The edit 93:101 didn’t cover the original tail of the constructor, so the old lines stayed underneath the new ones. The constructor now sets a random xid, then calls super().__init__() again and ends with self.xid = xid, which overwrites it with None. Every v0x04 Header created without an explicit xid now has xid = None. That’s worse than before, since it previously at least had a fixed int, and it may break packing. The edit output showed the duplicated lines at 109–112, and the agent didn’t notice.

The fix is also likely incomplete at the message level. Messages like GroupMod and MeterMod declare header = Header(...) as a class attribute, so that Header is built once at import time. The agent looked at these and concluded they’d “automatically use the updated behavior,” but without generating the xid in the message constructor (GenericMessage.__init__), instances of the same message type can still share an xid. It never checked base.py.

Tool use was reasonable navigation, searching for random and walking through each hit, but it didn’t read its own edit output. Reasoning was half right: it understood the root cause, but it never reproduced the problem (creating two headers or messages and comparing their xids) and never ran the tests.

Between the v0x04 regression and the message-level gap, I’d expect this to fail.

The fix is correct and is one of the solutions the issue itself proposes. Adding __reduce__ to _FixedOffset makes pickle rebuild it with the offset in minutes, replacing the inherited tzinfo.__reduce__, which called __init__ with no args. The repro now round-trips cleanly.

It’s not a 5 because the patch is sloppy:

dst is now defined twice. It’s harmless, since the second definition wins, but it’s obviously a botched edit.
There’s no blank line between __reduce__ and the module-level try: that follows, which flake8/pylint would flag.
total_seconds() / 60 produces a float. That works with timedelta(minutes=...), but // 60 or int(...) would be cleaner.

Tool use was mostly fine, apart from the edit. It wasted a step on a src directory that doesn’t exist, then re-ran the exact same failing edit right after the tool said not to. When it finally landed, it targeted the wrong line, which produced the duplicate dst, and it didn’t notice in the output.

Reasoning followed the full loop: it reproduced the exact error from the issue, diagnosed the missing init args, fixed it, and re-ran to confirm the round trip. Two small gaps: it only tested a GMT/zero-offset string, not something like +05:30, and it didn’t run the existing serialization tests.

The hidden test is almost certainly a pickle round-trip on deserialize_rfc output, which this handles. I’d expect it to pass unless a test constructs _FixedOffset with a timedelta directly.

The patch stops the crash. In finalize_vars, the nested-typedef branch assumes every variable belongs to a method and reads var["method"]["path"], but aCInstance is a class property with no method key. The agent’s guard falls back to the bare tag, the repro runs, and raw_type comes out as C.

The question is whether C is the right value. For a typedef nested inside class A, the qualified type is really A::C. That’s what the existing code builds for the method case, and it’s what the neighboring branches build for nested structs and enums. A fix that resolves the path from the property’s parent class would be more correct than dropping the qualifier. The nestedEnum and nestedStruct branches just above have the same var["method"] assumption and would crash the same way for class properties, and the agent didn’t touch them. The long one-line conditional is also a bit ugly, but that’s minor.

Tool use was clean and efficient. It reproduced the bug, found the file, went straight to the crashing line, made one edit, and re-ran. There was no thrashing and no junk left behind.

Reasoning followed reproduce → fix → verify, but it treated “no more KeyError” as success. The agent called raw_type = 'C' “the expected behavior” without checking what value the rest of the parser produces for nested types, and it never ran the existing test suite.

If the hidden test just parses this header and checks it doesn’t crash, or checks the property’s type, this passes. If it asserts raw_type == "A::C", it fails. I genuinely can’t tell which, so I’m just above even.

It stops the crash, but the new expression doesn’t mean what the agent thinks. Python’s conditional expression has the lowest precedence of any operator here, so the line parses as:

(tags[baseline] or ref_heads[baseline][len(base):]) if ref_heads[baseline] is not None else (baseline[:7] or baseline[:7])

When the baseline has a tag but no branch head, which is a very common case with -A, the tag is now thrown away and the name falls back to the short SHA. That’s a behavior regression: before, it only crashed when both were missing and the tag check failed. The trailing or baseline[:7] is also now effectively dead, and the line is long enough to fail lint. The clean fix is a one-liner like (ref_heads[baseline] or "")[len(base):] that keeps the original or chain intact.

Tool use was efficient, four steps to the right line, and the agent went straight where the issue pointed. But it made a single edit and never looked at the result critically.

Reasoning was minimal. It didn’t reproduce anything, even though a quick unit-level check with mocked tags/ref_heads dicts would have been easy. It didn’t think through how the or/if-else precedence would evaluate, and it didn’t run the existing experiments command tests. “The issue does not include specific reproduction steps, we’ll proceed to submit” is not a verification.

If the hidden test only covers the both-None case, this passes. If it checks that a tag still wins when there’s no branch head, it fails. That’s a coin flip.

The final patch is exactly right: a one-line change to the Capturs class’s __destto__ from ['OGLT24', 'OGLT24-1'] to ['OGCAPT', 'OGCAPT-1']. It also has a nice side effect the agent never mentions. Both LiveTrack24 and Capturs were registered under OGLT24, so Capturs was silently overwriting the LiveTrack24 parser in the registry. Fixing the callsign restores LT24 parsing too. The diff is clean, with no junk left behind.

Getting there was painful. The edit tool’s linter rejected the change because of pre-existing \d escape-sequence warnings in the file’s regexes, which had nothing to do with the edit. The agent then:

ran the exact same failing edit four times in a row, despite the tool explicitly saying not to,
searched for \d twice, which matched every “d” in the file, and then searched for the literal text “escape sequence”,
copied the whole file to parser_fixed.py, hit the same linter on the copy, and finally used sed,
deleted the original parser.py and moved the copy over it. That’s risky, and a direct sed -i on the original would have done the job in one step.

It also misread its own first sed: it said it replaced “the first occurrence,” but OGLT24 matched the start of both entries on the line. The end result happened to be correct anyway.

Reasoning was thin. The fix was spelled out in the issue, so diagnosis was trivial, but there was no reproduction (parsing an OGCAPT message) and no run of the parser tests afterward. The agent also chased the linter warnings as if they were real problems blocking the change instead of recognizing a tool quirk and going straight to a workaround.

The patch is correct and will very likely pass. The trajectory is a poor example of how to get there.

The patch makes the issue’s single example return [1], but it doesn’t fix the underlying problem. The new np.searchsorted(sorted_p, x) - 1 returns the index of the interval in sorted point order, not the element index from self.t. Those happen to match for a once-refined unit line, but refinement doesn’t keep elements numbered left to right. Refine twice, or use adaptive refinement, and the element ordering diverges from spatial ordering, so this returns the wrong element. The actual bug is in mapping a sorted interval back to the element that contains it, and the original == self.t[1] comparison was a broken attempt at exactly that mapping. The agent deleted that mapping instead of fixing it.

It also introduces a new boundary bug. With searchsorted’s default left side, x = 0 (the left endpoint) gives 0 - 1 = -1. The old digitize-based code didn’t have that problem. Smaller issues:

an unused n = self.p.shape[1] line,
the finder still mutates the caller’s x in place,
reproduce_bug.py is still committed. It deleted the second repro script but forgot the first.

Tool use was meandering. It created two repro scripts for the same thing, ran goto 499 while the repro file was open, and scrolled through the generic base class looking for MeshLine methods when a search would have been faster. It also spent several steps reading refined/_uniform, then didn’t use what it learned.

Reasoning started well with a solid reproduction, but the fix was trial and error. The first attempt returned -1, the second returned 1, and the agent declared victory. It never asked why t ordering matters, never tested other points (0, 0.25, 1.0) or a twice-refined mesh, and never ran the existing mesh tests. The issue’s own second example, comparing against a mesh rebuilt from sorted points, was a hint that ordering is the core problem.

Hidden tests will likely check element_finder across several refinement levels and points, so I’d expect this to fail.

The plumbing is reasonable. The agent added a parameter to the CustomObservable decorator, passed it through _custom_observable_builder, and set it as _id_contributing_properties on the generated class, which is where the built-in SCOs define it. But several things weaken it.

The kwarg name is a guess. The agent invented id_contributing_properties=. The library’s actual API for this, as far as I know, is id_contrib_props=. Hidden tests will call the decorator with the project’s chosen name, and any mismatch is a straight TypeError. This is the biggest risk.
Determinism was never checked. The whole point of the issue is deterministic IDs. The agent never created two instances with the same contributing property values to confirm they get the same ID. It also never looked at base.py, which showed up in its very first search, to see how _id_contributing_properties is actually consumed or whether a None value is handled safely.
__init__ is now duplicated in _CustomObservable. It’s harmless, since the second definition wins, but it’s leftover from a botched edit that the diff makes obvious.
No validation that the listed properties actually exist on the custom class.

Tool use was decent. It found the decorator, followed the import to custom.py after the first TypeError, and fixed the indentation error on the second try. The test script was cleaned up.

Reasoning stopped at “it doesn’t crash.” The test script only defines the class and prints a success message. It never instantiates an object, never compares IDs, and never runs the existing custom-object tests.

Given the likely kwarg-name mismatch with the hidden tests and the unverified behavior, I’d expect this to fail.

The fix is correct for the reported case. freeze dispatches on exact type (type(o) is dict), so a defaultdict falls through and comes back unchanged. The agent added a defaultdict branch that builds a pmap and recursively freezes the values, so in the issue’s example the nested dicts become pmaps too. It’s minimal and leaves no junk behind.

A few small things kept it from a 5:

The new branch duplicates the dict line instead of folding into it (if typ is dict or typ is defaultdict or ...).
The docstring list (“dict is converted to pmap...”) wasn’t updated to mention defaultdict.
thaw wasn’t considered, though the issue doesn’t ask for it.

Tool use was fine. find_file "freeze" was the wrong tool, since that searches filenames, but it recovered with search_dir right away and followed the import to _helpers.py. The first edit failed on the missing import. The second rewrote lines 1–45 just to add one import line, which is heavier than needed, but it landed cleanly.

Reasoning followed the full loop. It reproduced the exact output from the issue, found the type-dispatch cause, fixed it, and re-ran to get PMap. It only checked the outer type, not that the nested values were frozen, and it didn’t run freeze_test.py, which was sitting right there in the search results.

A hidden test for freezing a defaultdict, including nested values, should pass with this.

The fix the issue points at is simple: accept **kwargs in PureInterfaceType.__new__ and pass them through to super().__new__, in both places where it’s called. type.__new__ already calls __init_subclass__ with those kwargs. The submitted patch gets this wrong in several ways:

__init_subclass__ runs twice. The kwargs are never passed to super().__new__, so type.__new__ calls __init_subclass__() with no kwargs, and then the agent calls cls.__init_subclass__(**kwargs) manually afterwards. Any __init_subclass__ that requires a keyword will still fail on the first call, and any with side effects runs twice.

Changing test_nested_functions from 4 to 3 is correct under the spec, since a boolean operator inside a lambda shouldn’t pick up a nesting bonus. But the agent didn’t really argue why it was right; it changed the number because the test failed. It also left that test’s inline comment saying “+2 for or because lambda increases nesting,” which now contradicts the expected value.
The “# not 11” and “# not 4” comments are noise in a real commit.

Tool use was efficient. It found the test, traced from conftest.py to api.py to utils/ast.py, made one targeted edit, and ran the full suite each time. The one slip was trying to edit the test while ast.py was open; the linter caught it, and the agent fixed it on the next step.

Reasoning had the right loop: update the expectation, see it fail, find the cause, fix it, run the whole suite. Using the real test suite as verification is the best verification we’ve seen in this batch. The weak point is accepting the second failure by changing its expected value without checking it against the spec, though it happened to be right.

The hidden tests almost certainly expect these two updated values, so this should pass.

The fix is exactly right. In APISpec.__init__, plugins’ init_spec(self) ran before self.components was created, so a plugin couldn’t touch spec.components during init. Creating Components(...) first and then calling init_spec on each plugin solves it. Components only needs the plugins tuple and the OpenAPI version, both available at that point, so the reorder is safe. That’s essentially the canonical fix.

The one blemish is that the old # Components comment is left dangling at the end of __init__ with nothing under it. The agent removed the old line but not its comment.

Tool use was roundabout. find_file "APISpec" searches filenames, not contents, so it found nothing. It then opened plugin.py, opened core.py, decided APISpec wasn’t there, checked __init__.py, reopened core.py, and scrolled twice to reach the class. A single search_file "class APISpec" would have landed on it immediately. The second edit, deleting the old initialization line, was correct and clean.

Reasoning is the weak spot. It identified the ordering problem correctly, but it never reproduced it: a tiny plugin whose init_spec reads spec.components would have shown the AttributeError before and success after. It also didn’t run the test suite, even though tests/ is right there and a reorder in a constructor is exactly the kind of change that could affect other tests.

A hidden test where a plugin accesses spec.components in init_spec will pass.

The core idea is in the patch: self._entities[entity] = {} is now created before the component loop, so an entity made with no components does exist. But getting there introduced two real regressions:

Entity IDs now skip. The original code already did self._next_entity_id += 1 and then entity = self._next_entity_id. The agent’s edit 216:230 started its replacement below those lines and added its own increment, so each call now bumps the counter twice. Entities come out as 1, 3, 5… Anything that relies on sequential IDs, including the issue’s own entity_2 == 2 example, breaks.
The query cache isn’t cleared anymore. The self.clear_cache() call at the end of the loop was dropped in the rewrite. After create_entity(Position()), a previously cached get_component(Position) query can return stale results that miss the new entity. That would break existing processor and query tests.

It also left an unreachable second return in entity_exists, which does nothing but makes the diff confusing.

Tool use was okay at first (found the file, searched for the method), but each edit replaced a wider line range without checking what it deleted, which is how the extra increment and the missing clear_cache slipped in.

Reasoning broke down at the end. The repro script asserted the issue’s buggy behavior (assert not world.entity_exists(entity)) as if it were expected. After the fix, that assertion correctly failed, and the agent said “The assertion error indicates that the issue has been completely fixed” without checking which line failed. It never ran the existing test suite, which would have caught both regressions immediately.

A hidden test for empty entities might pass in isolation, but the ID skipping and stale cache will very likely break other tests.

The patch misreads the issue and breaks every STIX object’s ID.

The issue is about selectors. A granular marking’s selectors list points at property names, and "id" is a valid property to mark. SelectorProperty.clean rejects it because SELECTOR_REGEX is too strict for such a short name (it appears to require at least three characters for the first path segment). The fix belongs in SELECTOR_REGEX, so that short names like id are accepted.

The agent instead changed IDProperty.clean, the validator for object identifiers like indicator--<uuid>, and that does two bad things:

It applies the selector regex to object IDs, which have nothing to do with selectors.
It returns the result of _validate_id(...), which validates and returns nothing. Previously the code called it and then return value. Now clean returns None, so every object’s id is silently set to None during construction. That breaks essentially the whole library.

The agent read the issue as “the ID doesn’t conform to selector syntax, so make IDs validate against the selector regex,” which is backwards. It also invented a scenario where “the ID starts with a number,” which the issue never mentions.

The trajectory wandered: two GranularMarking classes, _STIXBase20 across three base.py files, a 45-hit search for "id", and none of it went near SelectorProperty or SELECTOR_REGEX, even though step 2 opened the file right at that regex. There was no repro (creating a GranularMarking(selectors=["id"], ...) takes one line), and the agent said “we cannot directly run a test script here,” which isn’t true, then submitted.

This fails, and it would also break nearly every existing test.

The fix is right. Click passes (ctx, param, value) to option callbacks, and the 2-argument form triggers that deprecation warning. Changing validate_orcid_id(ctx, orcid_id) to validate_orcid_id(ctx, param, orcid_id) is exactly what’s needed, and it’s the only callback in the file.

Two small problems:

Possible other callers. The agent didn’t check whether validate_orcid_id is called directly anywhere else, in the code or the tests, with the old two-argument signature. If it is, those calls now break.
Lint. The edit dropped a blank line, so there’s only one blank line before the @click.command decorator. flake8 would flag that as E302.

Tool use wandered early. It searched the repo for handle_parse_result, which is click’s internal function and was never going to be in this project, twice. It then tried a search_internet command that doesn’t exist. Searching for “click” got it to the right file, and the file search for click showed the callback right away.

Reasoning was weak on verification. The issue names the exact test that produces the warning (tests/test_setup_profile.py::test_provided_keypair_copied_to_nanopub_dir), and the agent said “we don’t have a specific test to run” and submitted. Running that one test with warnings shown would have confirmed the fix in seconds and also caught any broken direct calls.

The hidden test likely just checks that no warning fires (or that the profile setup still works), so this should pass.

The patch special-cases the test data instead of fixing anything, and it breaks existing behavior along the way.

unknown() now hard-codes an exception for 't' and 's'. That’s backwards from the issue: the reporter wants a free-standing t or s flagged as misspelled. The real problem is that contractions like “don’t” get split into don + t, so those fragments show up as errors. The agent made the repro output look clean by silencing two letters. Any genuine typo that happens to be a single t or s now goes unreported.
split_words() no longer uses the configured tokenizer. It used to call self._tokenizer(text), which can be swapped out by the user. Replacing that with a hard-coded re.findall silently ignores custom tokenizers, which existing tests likely cover.
Words are no longer lowercased. The original tokenizer lowercased, and the new output shows "That's" with a capital T. Callers and tests that expect lowercase tokens will break.
Other sloppiness. There’s an import re inside the method, and the \b added in the second regex change does nothing.

The right fix is in the tokenizer (_parse_into_words in utils.py): keep apostrophes inside words, so “don’t” stays one token, and keep lowercasing, so contractions are looked up as whole words.

Tool use had problems. The agent ran the same failing edit three times in a row, passing a regex= keyword the tokenizer doesn’t accept, and got the same TypeError each time before switching approaches. Navigation itself was fine.

Reasoning was poor. At the very first repro, the output {'t', 's'} already matched the issue’s second scenario, and the agent never stated clearly what correct output should look like. It then iterated until the set came back empty, rather than until the behavior was right. It never ran the existing test suite.

This fails, and it likely breaks existing tokenizer tests too.

This is exactly the fix the issue asks for. check_senza_version builds the upgrade command shown in the outdated-version warning, and both branches (the user install under /home and the system install with sudo) now say pip3, matching the README. It’s a minimal, clean diff with no junk left behind.

Tool use was efficient. The literal-message search found nothing, because the string is built with .format(), and the agent recognized that. It searched for the package name instead, found root.py, opened it, scrolled once to the command strings, and made a single edit.

The weak spot is verification. The agent’s own search showed tests/test_subcommands/test_root.py with three matches for stups-senza. Those are almost certainly assertions on this exact warning text, still expecting pip. It didn’t open them, update them, or run them, and it said “we cannot directly run the application,” which isn’t true, since pytest was right there. In the real repo, those existing tests would now fail until they’re updated to pip3.

The hidden tests will expect pip3, so the source change should pass. I’d note that the in-repo tests weren’t updated to match.

The crash is gone, but the fix substitutes the wrong value. The root cause is in path_splitter: PurePath('.').parts is an empty tuple, so *path_parts, base = s.parts has nothing to unpack. The right fix is to handle the empty-parts case there, for example by falling back to base = str(s) with no path parts, so '.' sorts as '.'.

Instead, the patch replaces '.' with os.getcwd(). That has real problems:

The sort key depends on the environment. '.' now sorts as if it were /natsort or whatever directory you happen to run from, so os_sorted(['.', 'a']) can give different orders on different machines. A test that checks the output of path_splitter('.') or a specific sort order will likely fail.
The same hack is applied in three places. It’s in the module-level _split_apply, in a new duplicate _split_apply nested inside the Windows-only os_sort_keygen, and in path_splitter itself. The two _split_apply edits were dead ends; they didn’t fix the crash, but they were left in.
Smaller issues. import os now runs inside hot functions on every call, and the Windows branch lost its blank-line formatting.

Tool use was clumsy. It used relative paths that the tool rejected, twice, and went back to absolute paths. It made five edit attempts that hit undefined names (_winsort_key, os, base, path_parts) because the line ranges cut into the code around them. It edited natsort.py twice before checking where the exception was actually raised, which the issue’s traceback already pointed to: utils.py, in path_splitter.

Reasoning had a good start with a clean repro of the exact error, but the fix came from trial and error. The first two edits didn’t change the error at all, and the agent kept them anyway. It never thought about what sort key '.' should have, and it never ran the existing tests.

A hidden test that checks how path_splitter or os_sorted handles '.' will probably fail.
